content: Advertising of breast-milk substitutes, including the display or distribution of materials or equipment bearing the branding of manufacturers of such substitutes, is strictly prohibited. This includes the provision of discount coupons or free samples of infant formula to mothers for use within healthcare facilities or to take home. These practices align with the WHO Guidance on ending the inappropriate promotion of foods for infants and young children, published in 2016 and endorsed by the World Health Assembly (WHA). Healthcare workers and systems must avoid conflicts of interest with companies marketing infant and young child foods. Healthcare professional meetings should not be sponsored by industry, and industry representatives should not participate in parenting education. All infant formula, feeding bottles, and teats used in healthcare facilities must be procured through standard procurement channels and not received as free or subsidized supplies. Facilities must not display products covered under the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes or items bearing the logos of companies producing such products. Facilities must have a written policy detailing adherence to the Code, including procurement practices, refusal of gifts or support from manufacturers or distributors, and prohibition of providing free samples of breast-milk substitutes, feeding bottles, or teats to mothers. At least 80% of healthcare professionals providing antenatal, delivery, or newborn care should be able to explain at least two elements of the Code. Healthcare facilities providing maternity and newborn services must have a written breastfeeding policy that is routinely communicated to staff and parents. This policy should outline the implementation of clinical and care practices to ensure consistent application for all mothers. It should also include management procedures institutionalized through specific processes. Facilities must establish ongoing monitoring and data-management systems to track key clinical practices, such as early initiation of breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding. These indicators, considered sentinel indicators, should be routinely tracked for each mother-infant pair. Data collection should be incorporated into medical charts and relevant registers. The group or committee coordinating Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI)-related activities within a facility should review progress at least every six months. During periods of quality improvement, monthly reviews are necessary. The purpose of these reviews is to track indicator values, assess whether targets are met, and implement corrective actions if needed. Facilities should aim for at least 80% compliance with all process and outcome indicators, including early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding. If compliance falls below this threshold, clinical practices and management procedures should be assessed to identify bottlenecks and implement necessary improvements. Healthcare staff providing infant feeding services, including breastfeeding support, must have sufficient knowledge, competence, and skills to support women in breastfeeding. This includes pre-service or in-service training and competency assessments. Training should focus on practical skills, such as counseling mothers, assessing breastfeeding, and addressing common breastfeeding challenges. Pregnant women and their families should be counseled on the benefits and management of breastfeeding during antenatal care. This includes information on the importance of breastfeeding, risks of formula feeding, and national recommendations for infant feeding. Practical skills, such as positioning, attachment, and recognizing feeding cues, should also be taught. Facilities must ensure that at least 80% of healthcare professionals providing antenatal, delivery, or newborn care have received training on breastfeeding within the past two years and can correctly answer questions on breastfeeding knowledge and skills. The updated BFHI emphasizes eight key clinical practices to support breastfeeding, based on the WHO Guideline on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services. These practices include discussing breastfeeding with pregnant women, providing timely support for breastfeeding initiation, and addressing common breastfeeding challenges. Healthcare facilities must ensure that all staff assisting mothers with infant feeding are assessed on their ability to counsel mothers effectively, help with breastfeeding positioning and attachment, and address specific challenges such as low milk supply, engorgement, or sore nipples. Facilities should provide up-to-date information on best practices for maternity and newborn care, including skin-to-skin contact and other practices that facilitate successful breastfeeding.
